html:
Equatorial Guinea is a small country on the west coast of Central Africa, the only one in Africa where Spanish is official. It has two parts: the island of Bioko in the Gulf of Guinea and the mainland of Río Muni, between Cameroon and Gabon.

Portugal handed its claim to Bioko, then called Fernando Po, and Annobón to Spain in 1778, in exchange for land in South America. Spain did little with them at first. From 1827 to the 1840s Britain used Bioko as a base for its navy's patrols after it banned the slave trade. The mainland borders were settled with France in 1900.

As Spanish Guinea, the colony grew cocoa on Bioko plantations. Planters brought in contract workers from Liberia and Nigeria under harsh conditions. The island's people are the Bubi; the mainland is mostly Fang.

  • 1968: independence.
  • 1968 to 1979: Francisco Macías Nguema ruled by terror. A large share of the population fled or was killed.
  • 1979: his nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo overthrew and executed him. He has ruled since.
  • 1990s: offshore oil made the country one of the richest in Africa per head on paper, while most people stayed poor.

Malabo on Bioko was the capital until January 2026, when the government moved to the new mainland city of Ciudad de la Paz.
sum: Equatorial Guinea is a small country on the west coast of Central Africa, the only one in Africa where Spanish is official. It has two parts: the island of Bioko in the Gulf of Guinea and the mainland of Río Muni, between Cameroon and Gabon…
